C0.quote: In this paper we introduce a new voting formalism to support
C0.note: Approval-based voting rules for sequences of collective decisions (perpetual voting).

C1.quote: voting rules via an axiomatic analysis as well as a quantitative
C1.note: Main results are axiomatic (Props 1-5, Thms 1-4) and simulations on synthetic 2D Euclidean data. OT: the paper names the introduction of the perpetual voting formalism, axioms and metrics as its main contribution (modelling proposal). Polynomial-time computability is only a one-line remark, not coded AL.

C2.3.quote: voters to misrepresent their preferences (or abstain)
C2.3.note: Preferences distinct from the submitted approval set are referred to in the Discussion; the simulations also give voters positions in the plane from which approval sets are generated (Section 6, p. 2108).

C2.4.quote: voters to misrepresent their preferences (or abstain)
C2.4.note: Doubt with IDU: in the formal model (Sections 2-3) the approval profile itself is called 'the preferences in Ak+1' and the rule is applied to it with no reporting statement; only the Discussion says submitted inputs may differ from preferences. DIST listed first.

C3.1.quote: It requires further work to understand the impact of the
C3.1.note: Strategic misreporting (freerider effect) is only mentioned as future work in Section 7; no analysis models it. The 'fake decisions' motivation of Definition 3 concerns agenda manipulation, not voter misreporting.

C3.2.loc: Checked: Abstract and Section 1 (p. 2103-2104), Section 2 model (p. 2104), Section 3 (pp. 2105-2106), Section 6 (p. 2108), Section 7 conclusion (pp. 2109-2110)
C3.2.note: Section 2 only says voters approve a subset; no statement that approvals are sincere.

C4.1.quote: the voters’ utility is their satisfaction if their satisfaction is
C4.1.note: Satisfaction is defined as the number of rounds in which the chosen alternative is approved; for Perpetual Nash utility is defined as this satisfaction (epsilon if 0). Simulations also generate approvals from a spatial model (Section 6).

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' or an equivalent is not used.

C5.1.quote: degree voters receive at least a “fair share” of favorable
C5.1.note: Claims about proportionality/fairness to voters and minorities, voter satisfaction, influence inequality (Gini) and Nash welfare.

C5.2.quote: The satisfaction of voter v ∈ N in round j is
C5.2.note: Satisfaction, quota, influence and Nash welfare are all computed from approval profiles; the paper does not state that approvals equal held preferences nor that the evaluation is with respect to reported inputs.

VOT.quote_behav: each voter v ∈ N approves some non-empty subset of C
VOT.note: Approval profiles are exogenous in all analyses; in the simulations voters' approvals follow a fixed distance rule (Section 6, p. 2108). Strategic behaviour (freerider effect) is only discussed as an open issue in Section 7.

CAN.note: Alternatives are objects, not agents; no candidate interests discussed.

ORG.note: Definition 3 is motivated by someone 'putting fake decisions on the agenda' (Section 1, p. 2104; Section 4, p. 2106), but no such agent is modelled.

DES.note: Rules are compared by the author; no designer choice or objective is modelled.

C9.2.quote: It requires further work to understand the impact of the
C9.2.note: Stated: utility/satisfaction defined from approvals (Def. 1, Perpetual Nash). Unstated: that submitted approval sets equal voters' held preferences, and that voters do not act strategically (the freerider effect is acknowledged in Section 7 but its impact is left open); the claim that minorities are incentivized to participate also needs an unstated behavioural assumption.
